title: Arithmetic without operators
sub: Sum of Two Integers and Divide Two Integers: column carries, division by shifts, int.MinValue / −1 and checked
cards/0/title: Sum of Two Integers: column addition
cards/0/body:
Sum of Two Integers (LeetCode #371): add a and b without the + and − operators; −1000 ≤ a, b ≤ 1000. The problem checks whether you understand how the processor itself adds.

Binary column addition: in each column 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 0 with a carry of 1 into the next column. “The sum without carries” is exactly a ^ b. Carries appear where both bits are 1 and move one column left: (a & b) << 1. Hence a + b = (a ^ b) + ((a & b) << 1) — a sum again, but the second term consists of carries only. Repeat until no carries are left.

Why the loop ends. The carry is shifted left, so each round it has at least one more trailing zero than before. In at most 32 rounds all its 1s move past bit 31 and the carry becomes 0.
cards/1/q: How many rounds of the loop does a = 7, b = 1 take?
cards/1/options/0: 4: the carry runs through the three 1s of 7, one column per round
cards/1/explain: 0111 + 0001. Round 1: a ^ b = 0110, carry 0010. Round 2: 0100 and carry 0100. Round 3: 0000 and carry 1000. Round 4: a = 1000, no carry. A run of 1s is the worst case for this loop: the carry walks through it column by column.
cards/1/wrong/1: The single 1 in b produces a carry, and that carry produces the next one while it runs over the 1s of a.
cards/1/wrong/2: The number of rounds depends not on the answer but on the length of the carry chain.
cards/2/q: Build the sum without a plus.
cards/2/explain: The loop runs while there are carries: b != 0. The carry is computed first, while a is still the old value: (a & b) << 1 — the columns where both are 1, moved one column left. Then a ^= b is the sum without carries, and the carries become the new b.
cards/3/title: Negatives: the carry falls off bit 31
cards/3/body:
The same loop adds negative numbers too, thanks to two’s complement. −5 = …11111011₂, 7 = 00000111₂. Carries appear in bits 1 and 2, then run left through the solid 1s of −5, one column per round. At bit 31 the carry goes past the edge of the register and simply disappears: << drops the bits it pushes out. That is not a bug: in two’s complement the sum is taken modulo 2³², and that is exactly how −5 + 7 = 2 comes out. It takes 31 rounds.

Hence the cost: 32 rounds in the worst case (−1 + 1), which is O(32) = O(1) at a fixed width. checked does not affect this code: ^, & and << never throw — overflow is only checked for arithmetic (+, −, *, /) and type conversions.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on a = −5, b = 7: the carry runs over the 1s of −5 all the way to bit 31. The rig asks about the second round and the last one.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Round 2: a = −4 = …11111100₂, b = 6 = 110₂. What comes out?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: a ^ b = …11111010 = −6. −4 and 6 share a single 1, bit 2, so the carry goes to bit 3: b = 8. The sum has not changed: −6 + 8 = 2. From here the carry keeps running left over the 1s of a, one column per round.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: a = 2, b = 0 — the carry fell off bit 31
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: a = 2, b = int.MinValue — the loop never ends
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: Round 31: the carry has reached bit 31 — b = int.MinValue, a = −2,147,483,646. What happens?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: a ^ b = 2: both have bit 31 set, and it cancels. a & b = int.MinValue — a 1 in bit 31 — and the left shift pushes it past the edge: the carry is 0 and the loop ends. No exception: shifts are not overflow-checked even in checked. −5 + 7 = 2 modulo 2³², the same way the processor adds.
cards/5/body:
Divide Two Integers (#29): divide without *, / and %, dropping the fraction — rounding toward zero: 7 / −3 = −2. The numbers span the whole int range, the divisor is not 0; if the quotient does not fit in an int, return int.MaxValue.

Brute force subtracts the divisor while it can: as many steps as the quotient, up to 2³¹ ≈ 2·10⁹ when dividing by 1 — too slow. The idea is binary long division: go from bit 31 down to 0 and ask whether b · 2ᵏ fits into what is left. If it does, subtract it and set bit k of the quotient. The test (a >> k) >= b is the same as a >= b · 2ᵏ, but cannot overflow. 32 steps — O(1) at a fixed width, O(log) in the value.

The sign goes separately: divide the absolute values; the quotient is negative if the signs differ. Take the absolute values in long: |int.MinValue| = 2³¹ does not fit in an int.
cards/6/body:
The only quotient that does not fit in an int is int.MinValue / −1 = 2³¹. In .NET this division throws OverflowException even without checked, and so does int.MinValue % −1. The C# standard leaves the unchecked behaviour to the implementation, and .NET chose the exception. That is why #29 checks this case first.

Two more places. Math.Abs(int.MinValue) throws OverflowException. And -x with x == int.MinValue silently returns int.MinValue — a negative “absolute value”. The safe way is to widen to long before taking the absolute value: Math.Abs((long)x).

checked helps find such spots in tests: overflow in addition, subtraction, multiplication and conversions becomes an exception. Shifts and bitwise operations are left alone.
cards/6/code:
int min = int.MinValue, m1 = -1;
int q = min / m1;                 // OverflowException, even without checked
int abs = Math.Abs(min);          // OverflowException
int neg = -min;                   // -2147483648: silently
long ok = Math.Abs((long)min);    // 2147483648
cards/7/q: This Divide throws OverflowException for dividend = int.MinValue, divisor = 2. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: Math.Abs(dividend) is called on an int and fails on int.MinValue before the result ever reaches the long: the absolute value 2³¹ does not fit in an int. Widen first, then take the absolute value: Math.Abs((long)dividend).
cards/8/body:
x << k = x · 2ᵏ, with the same wrap-around as unchecked multiplication. x >> k divides by 2ᵏ rounding down, while / rounds toward zero: −7 >> 1 = −4, but −7 / 2 = −3. For non-negative numbers they are the same.

There is no need to write x >> 1 instead of x / 2 “for speed”: the JIT (and the C++ compiler behind IL2CPP) turns division by a power-of-two constant into a shift by itself, with a sign fix-up for int. Replacing it by hand, though, changes the meaning for negatives. The same goes for the remainder: −3 % 2 == −1, so the odd test x % 2 == 1 is false for negatives — write (x & 1) != 0 or x % 2 != 0.

The remainder by a power of two is a mask: x & (m − 1) instead of x % m for non-negative x. This is how a ring buffer of size 2ᵏ (frame history, a network packet queue) computes its index — no division and no negative remainders.
cards/8/code:
int x = -7;
int a = x / 2;                  // -3: toward zero
int b = x >> 1;                 // -4: down
bool odd1 = x % 2 == 1;         // false: -7 % 2 == -1
bool odd2 = (x & 1) != 0;       // true
int head = 1029;
int slot = head & (1024 - 1);   // 5: same as head % 1024, a buffer of 1024 = 2^10
cards/9/q: Which equalities hold for every int x (unchecked)? Select all.
cards/9/explain: Multiplying by 8 and shifting by 3 give the same 32 bits with the same wrap-around. Division and shift disagree on negative odd numbers: −7 / 2 = −3, −7 >> 1 = −4. The remainder disagrees on negatives: −5 % 8 = −5, but −5 & 7 = 3. −x = ~x + 1 is the definition of two’s complement and holds even for int.MinValue. Math.Abs(int.MinValue) returns nothing — it throws OverflowException.
cards/10/q: You are solving Divide Two Integers out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: rounding toward zero, the int range, what to return on overflow
cards/10/items/1: Brute force: subtract the divisor — up to 2³¹ steps when dividing by 1
cards/10/items/2: Idea: long division — from bit 31 down, subtract b · 2ᵏ when it fits
cards/10/items/3: Code: the int.MinValue / −1 case first, absolute values in long, the sign separately
cards/10/items/4: Run it: 7 / −3 → |7| = 111₂, |−3| = 11₂: at k = 1 subtract 6, remainder 1 → 2, negative sign → −2
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: int.MinValue as dividend and divisor, a divisor of ±1
cards/10/explain: The special case int.MinValue / −1 comes up while clarifying the problem and goes on the first line of code: it is the only one that does not fit in an int. Running a small signed example checks both the long division and the rounding toward zero.
cards/11/title: Multiplying with shifts, and how the processor does it
cards/11/body:
If * is banned too, multiplication is split over the bits of the multiplier: x · y = the sum of x · 2ᵏ over the 1s of y. It is the same long-hand scheme as in division, just the other way round: 32 steps, each a shift and maybe an addition.

The sum loop from this lesson is a software version of a carry running through the digits. A real adder computes the carries for all digits in parallel and adds in a single cycle, while division is one of the slowest integer operations in a processor: from about ten to a few dozen cycles, against one for an addition. That is why compilers replace division by a constant with a multiplication and a shift.
cards/11/deep:
#29 without long. The strict version of the problem allows 32-bit numbers only. Then you keep both numbers negative: −2³¹ has no positive counterpart, but every positive int has a negative one. Double the divisor while d >= (int.MinValue >> 1) — then d + d cannot overflow — and compare “backwards”: a <= d means |a| ≥ |d|. The quotient is accumulated as a negative too and negated at the end; the only case where that overflows is int.MinValue / −1, which was handled first.

Division by a constant. The JIT turns x / 10 into a multiplication by a “magic” number and a shift of the high half of the product — several times faster than the divide instruction. For uint and division by 2ᵏ it is just a shift; for int it is a shift with a fix-up so that it rounds toward zero.

.NET and Unity. Math.DivRem returns the quotient and the remainder in one call; Math.BigMul(int, int) gives the exact 64-bit product. Division is expensive in Burst code too: hot loops over a grid often use power-of-two sizes so that / and % become a shift and a mask — like the ring buffer index above.
